correct_citation: Jacob, R. T., Armstrong, C., & Willard, J. A. (2015, March). A., & Rifkin, R. E., June 2014, "Reading Partners: The Implementation and Effectiveness of a One-on-One Tutoring Program Delivered by Community Volunteers," MDRC Policy Brief.)
design: Randomized controlled trial; students randomly assigned within schools and grade groups (2-3, 4-5) to Reading Partners or business-as-usual control
population_location: 1,265 randomized / 1,166 analyzed (594 program, 572 control) struggling readers in grades 2-5, 19 schools in California, New York and Washington, DC, 2012-13
outcome: Reading comprehension (SAT-10), fluency (AIMSweb), sight-word efficiency (TOWRE-2)

note: Sample, design and effect sizes all match. Average of 2.5 tutors confirmed (Table 3.2: 2.52 tutors assigned). The cause differs: the report says students usually had two tutors by design, because tutors often come once a week. Turnover and absences added more. The cited brief is dated June 2014 and is by Jacob, Smith, Willard & Rifkin; Jacob, Armstrong & Willard is the March 2015 full report.

correct_citation: Black, A. R., Somers, M.-A., Doolittle, F., Unterman, R., & Grossman, J. B. (2009). The Evaluation of Enhanced Academic Instruction in After-School Programs: Final Report (NCEE 2009-4077). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, IES, U.S. Department of Education.
design: Two-stage randomized trial: students randomly assigned by grade within each after-school center to the enhanced program or the regular after-school program, in two school years
population_location: Students in grades 2-5 who were below grade level (by no more than two years) at 27 after-school centers that took part in both years (15 math, 12 reading), 2005-06 and 2006-07, US
outcome: SAT 10 total math and total reading scores
effect_as_reported: Math, one year (Cohort 1): +3.5 scaled score points = 0.09 SD (significant). Cohort 2: 3.4 points (not significant). Two-year offer: 2.0 points (p = 0.52), no added benefit over one year. Reading: no one-year impact; two-year offer had a negative, significant impact.

note: The math results come from the 15 math centers, not all 27. The 48 hours is the extra math instruction the enhanced group received over the control group in Cohort 1 (42 in Cohort 2), not the total dose. "No difference after two years" fits the math finding of no added benefit over the one-year effect. The claim leaves out that reading had no effect after one year and a significant negative effect after two.

correct_citation: Taylor, R. D., Oberle, E., Durlak, J. A., & Weissberg, R. P. (2017). Promoting Positive Youth Development Through School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Interventions: A Meta-Analysis of Follow-Up Effects. Child Development, 88(4), 1156-1171. doi:10.1111/cdev.12864

correct_citation: Goyer, J. P., Cohen, G. L., Cook, J. E., Master, A., Apfel, N., Lee, W., Henderson, A. G., Reeves, S. L., Okonofua, J. A., & Walton, G. M. (2019). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 117(2), 229-259. doi:10.1037/pspa0000152
design: Two randomized field experiments (student-level random assignment to treatment or control exercises)
population_location: Exp. 1: 669 students in 7th-8th grades at 2 middle schools with a large Latino population (US). Exp. 2: 137 sixth graders at a third school with a large Black population, followed through the end of high school
outcome: School discipline citations
effect_as_reported: Exp. 2: citations among Black boys -65% through the end of high school (95% CI -85% to -15%); the gap with White boys closed by 75% over 7 years. Experiment 1, in the Latino-majority schools, combined social-belonging, values-affirmation and growth-mindset exercises over several class sessions with 7th and 8th graders (N=669). It also had a growth-mindset-only arm (-70%). The 57% belongs to the combined treatment, not to a social-belonging exercise.

correct_citation: What Works Clearinghouse (2015, May). Dropout Prevention intervention report: Check & Connect (updated May 2015). Washington, DC: Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education.

correct_citation: Álvarez-Bueno, C., Pesce, C., Cavero-Redondo, I., Sánchez-López, M., Garrido-Miguel, M., & Martínez-Vizcaíno, V. (2017). Academic Achievement and Physical Activity: A Meta-analysis. Pediatrics, 140(6), e20171498. doi:10.1542/peds.2017-1498

correct_citation: Dunster, G. P., de la Iglesia, L., Ben-Hamo, M., Nave, C., Fleischer, J. G., Panda, S., & de la Iglesia, H. O. (2018). correct_citation: Dahl, G. B., & Lochner, L. (2012). The Impact of Family Income on Child Achievement: Evidence from the Earned Income Tax Credit. American Economic Review, 102(5), 1927-1956. Correction: Dahl, G. B., & Lochner, L. (2017). ... : Reply. American Economic Review, 107(2), 629-631. Comment that found the error: Lundstrom, S. (2017). ... : Comment. American Economic Review, 107(2), 623-628.
design: Instrumental variables using large nonlinear EITC changes (1993-1997) as the instrument for family income; panel data
population_location: About 4,500 children (4,412 children of 2,401 mothers) in the Children of the NLSY79, US
outcome: Combined PIAT math and reading test scores

correct_citation: Dougherty, S. M. (2018). The Effect of Career and Technical Education on Human Capital Accumulation: Causal Evidence from Massachusetts. Education Finance and Policy, 13(2), 119-148. doi:10.1162/edfp_a_00224

correct_citation: Mulolli, D., & Dickinson, E. R. (2026, June 10). Middle School Career Exploration Impact on High School CTE Outcomes (Report 2026 No. 064). Prepared for the Kentucky Department of Education, Office of Assessment and Accountability.

correct_citation: Fortson, J., James-Burdumy, S., Bleeker, M., Beyler, N., London, R. A., Westrich, L., Stokes-Guinan, K., & Castrechini, S. (2013, May). Impact and Implementation Findings from an Experimental Evaluation of Playworks: Effects on School Climate, Academic Learning, Student Social Skills and Behavior. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research; Stanford, CA: John W. Gardner Center for Youth and Their Communities.
design: School-level randomized controlled trial (29 schools matched into blocks; 17 treatment, 12 control), 2010-11 and 2011-12 cohorts
population_location: 29 low-income elementary schools in six US cities (25 schools in cohort 1, 4 in cohort 2); student survey of 2,331 4th-5th graders
outcome: Teacher- and student-reported school climate, bullying, transition to learning, behavior; academic proficiency; administrative attendance and discipline; physical activity (companion brief)

Student-survey results were mostly null, but students did report significantly better behavior and attention in class after play. The Mathematica and Gardner Center copies returned 404/403. "Six cities" is correct: the cohort 1 subset came from five.
